client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed by my new job at the tech startup. It seems like the demands are never-ending, and I constantly feel like I'm falling behind on my project deadlines. I'm starting to question whether I can keep up with everything, and I'm not sure if talking about it in therapy will actually help.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when starting a new job, especially in a fast-paced environment like a tech startup. Your feelings of questioning your ability to keep up are valid, and it's okay to explore those thoughts here. What do you think might happen if you shared these concerns in therapy?

client: I guess if I talked about my concerns, it might help me sort through my feelings. But I worry that it would just feel like complaining without any real solutions. Plus, I'm not sure if anyone can really understand the pressure I'm under or if they would just tell me to manage my time better, which feels impossible right now.
therapist: It's understandable to worry that discussing your feelings might come across as complaining, but sharing your experiences can often lead to valuable insights and solutions. It's also okay to feel that the pressure is overwhelming; many people struggle with similar feelings in high-demand environments. What are some specific pressures you’re experiencing that feel particularly challenging right now?

client: One of the biggest pressures I’m feeling is the constant need to prove myself. Everyone around me seems so confident and capable, and I can’t shake the feeling that I'm not measuring up. It makes me anxious about every little mistake, and I worry that if I don’t perform perfectly, I’ll let my team down. I just don’t see how talking about this will change anything.
therapist: Feeling the need to prove yourself in a new environment can be incredibly stressful, and it's important to acknowledge how that pressure is affecting your anxiety. It’s natural to compare yourself to others, but remember that everyone has their own struggles, even if they’re not visible. What might happen if you allowed yourself to make mistakes and view them as a part of your learning process instead?

client: I can see how viewing mistakes as part of the learning process could be helpful, but it’s hard for me to actually believe that. I just feel like I can’t afford to make any mistakes right now, especially when my job feels like it’s on the line. It’s like I’m stuck in this mindset where every error is a reflection of my worth, and I don’t know how to change that perspective.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that way, especially when the stakes feel so high. It's common to tie our self-worth to our performance, but that perspective can be quite limiting. What would it look like for you to separate your value as a person from your work performance, and how might that shift help you feel more at ease in your role?

client: I think separating my self-worth from my work performance would be really freeing, but it feels like such a big leap. I’m not sure how to start doing that, especially when my job feels like it defines me right now. It’s just hard to imagine feeling okay about myself when I’m constantly worried about meeting expectations at work.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that your job defines you, especially when you're in a demanding environment. Taking small steps toward separating your self-worth from your work can be a gradual process, and it’s okay to take your time with it. What are some qualities or strengths you possess outside of your job that you could acknowledge and appreciate more?

client: I guess I have some strengths outside of work, like being a good friend and being creative in my hobbies. But it feels like those qualities don't matter as much when I'm struggling professionally. When I think about acknowledging them, I worry that it will just feel like I'm trying to convince myself of something that isn't true. It’s hard to shift my focus away from work when that’s where all my energy is going right now.
therapist: It's great that you can identify those strengths, even if they feel overshadowed by your work struggles right now. It’s completely normal to feel that way when so much of your energy is focused on your job. Perhaps you could try setting aside even a small amount of time to engage in those hobbies or reach out to friends, allowing yourself to experience those positive aspects of your life. How do you think it might feel to intentionally carve out time for those activities, even just for a little while?

client: I think carving out time for my hobbies could feel refreshing, but I also worry that I won’t actually follow through. With everything going on at work, it feels like there's never enough time, and it’s hard to justify taking a break when I have so much to do. I guess I’m just afraid that if I step away, I’ll fall even further behind.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel hesitant about taking a break when work feels overwhelming, but sometimes stepping away can actually help you recharge and be more productive when you return. You don’t have to spend a lot of time on your hobbies—just a few moments can make a difference in your mood. What if you set a very small, specific goal, like 10 minutes of engaging in a hobby? How might that help you feel less guilty about taking a break?

client: I can see how just 10 minutes could be manageable, but I still feel that nagging guilt about not working during that time. It feels like I’ll be wasting precious minutes that could be spent catching up on my projects. Plus, I worry that once I start taking breaks, I might not want to go back to work at all.
therapist: It's completely normal to feel guilt about taking breaks, especially when there’s so much on your plate. However, those small moments of rest can actually boost your focus and creativity in the long run, which might help you tackle your projects more effectively. What if you considered those 10 minutes as a necessary investment in your well-being rather than a waste? How do you think you might feel about work after allowing yourself that brief pause?

client: I understand that taking those 10 minutes could help me feel more focused, but it still feels like a big mental shift for me. I worry that if I allow myself to take breaks, I might spiral into procrastination instead of using that time to recharge. It's frustrating because I want to believe that it could help, but I just can't see it clearly yet.
therapist: It's completely valid to feel apprehensive about making that mental shift, especially when you're concerned about procrastination. Acknowledging that fear is a good first step, and perhaps you could think of those 10 minutes as a structured break, setting a timer to help you return to your tasks afterward. How might it feel to experiment with that structure, even just once, and see how it impacts your energy and focus?

client: I see what you’re saying about the structured break, and it does sound like it could be worth trying just once. But I still feel this tightness in my chest at the thought of stepping away, like I’m somehow failing if I take that time. I’m worried that even if I set a timer, I might get distracted and lose track of time, which would just add to my anxiety about work.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that tightness and anxiety about taking a break, especially when you’re feeling so much pressure at work. It’s important to recognize that allowing yourself to step away doesn’t mean you’re failing; it’s about giving yourself the space to recharge so you can perform better. What if you tried a very brief break, maybe just a minute or two, to see how it feels? You could even set a timer for that short break to give you some reassurance that you'll return to your work right after. How does that idea sit with you?
